ety.text: From Middle English majeste, mageste, from Old French majesté, from Latin maiestātem, (literally, "the quality of being greater”). Ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *meǵh₂s (“great”) See mega-.

senses.d: The quality of being impressive, great, dignified, powerful, sovereign, or any combination thereof.
ex: the majesty of the Great Pyramids

ety.text: Latin maiorder. Middle English major English major From Middle English major, from Latin maior, comparative of magnus (“great, large; noble, important”), from Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂yōs (“greater”), comparative of *meǵh₂- (“great”). Compare West Frisian majoar (“major”), Dutch majoor (“major”), French majeur. Doublet of mayor. Noun sense 1 is a shortening of sergeant major, perhaps after Spanish mayor in the same sense.

senses.d: Greater in dignity, rank, importance, significance, or interest.
Greater in number, quantity, or extent.
ex: the major part of the assembly
The three major religions are Islam, Judaism, and Christianity.

senses.d: Notable or conspicuous in effect or scope.
ex: The building underwent a major renovation.

senses.d: Prominent or significant in size, amount, or degree.
ex: to earn some major cash
a major exhibition

senses.d: Involving great risk, serious, life-threatening.
ex: to suffer from a major illness

senses.d: Of full legal age, having attained majority.
ex: major children

senses.d: Of or relating to a subject of academic study chosen as a field of specialization.
Having intervals of a semitone between the third and fourth, and seventh and eighth degrees. (of a scale)
ex: major scale

senses.d: Equivalent to that between the tonic and another note of a major scale, and greater by a semitone than the corresponding minor interval. (of an interval)
ex: major third

senses.d: Having a major third above the root.
ex: major triad

senses.d: A rank of officer in the army and the US air force, between captain and lieutenant colonel.
ex: He used to be a major in the army.

senses.d: An officer in charge of a section of band instruments, used with a modifier.
A person of legal age.
A system of change-ringing using eight bells.
A large, commercially successful company, especially a record label that is bigger than an indie.
The principal subject or course of a student working toward a degree at a college or university.
ex: Midway through his second year of college, he still hadn't chosen a major.

senses.d: A student at a college or university specializing on a given area of study.
ex: She is a math major.

senses.d: A touchdown, or major score.
A goal.
An elder brother (especially at a public school).
Used in a phrasal verb: major in.

ety.text: Spanish mayorder. Middle French major French majorbor. Portuguese major Borrowed from French major. Doublet of maior and mor.
From maggiore + -enne.
From Middle French maiorité, from Medieval Latin maiōritātem, accusative of Latin maiōritās, from Latin maior (“greater”). Morphologically major + -ity.

senses.d: More than half (50%) of some group.
ex: The majority agreed that the new proposal was the best.
Those opposing the building plans were in the majority, so the building project was canceled.

senses.d: Any share or fraction that is bigger than any one of its counterpart shares or fractions (of the same whole).

In a parliament or legislature, the difference in seats between the ruling party and the opposition; (UK) in an election, the difference in votes between the winning candidate and the second-place candidate, or between the winning candidate and all of the other candidates combined.
ex: The ruling party had a narrow three-seat majority in the legislature.
The winner with 53% had a 6% majority over the loser with 47%.

senses.d: Legal adulthood, age of majority.
ex: By the time I reached my majority, I had already been around the world twice.

senses.d: The office held by a member of the armed forces in the rank of major.
ex: On receiving the news of his promotion, Charles Snodgrass said he was delighted to be entering his majority.

senses.d: Ancestors; ancestry.
ex: Of evil parents an evil generation, a posterity not unlike their majority; of mischievous progenitors, a venomous and destructive progeny.
